ARMY MEDICINE
STRATEGIC PLAN

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
3
FOREWORD
Army Medicine Leaders,
The Army Medical Regiment’s purpose is clear and enduring, supported by our unifying
culture. Collectively, Army Medicine provides combat ready care at the point of need to
build trust, inspire confidence, and enable the Army and Joint Force. This sacred mission
requires ownership and an understanding that medical leaders at echelon are accountable
and responsible for delivering expert medical care and advisement throughout the Army.
This establishes trust, and that trust is the cornerstone of everything we do.
Army Medicine is committed to Soldier health, readiness, and lethality across the conflict
continuum. This begins at home station by ensuring Soldiers are medically ready for
warfighting as the most lethal version of themselves (Soldier as a weapon system). Throughout
competition, this lethality is sustained through prevention, health promotion, and force health
protection. If deterrence fails, Army Medicine provides combat casualty care at the point
of need, clearing the battlefield, and returning Soldiers to the fight. Should Soldiers suffer
battle injuries, disease, or illness, Army Medicine is with them every step of the way through
rehabilitation. Army Medicine ensures force health protection and sustains the Warfighter
for multidomain operations, delivering a medical force that is combat ready in support
of Combatant Commanders. We are optimized to support warfighting, providing quality
healthcare, and leveraging the whole of government to fight and win our Nation’s wars.
A comprehensive strategic plan achieves this end by synchronizing ways and means
across commands and components. The Army Medicine Strategic Plan’s five Lines of Effort
are nested with the Army’s Continuous Transformation Campaign Plan: 1) Recruit, Build,
and Strengthen the Army Medicine Profession, 2) Transform Army Medicine for MDO and
the Future Fight, 3) Sustain Health, Medically Preserve and Reconstitute Combat Power,
4) Deliver Combat Ready Medical Forces, and 5) Strengthen Alliances and Partnerships.
This plan is centered on people, our strategic advantage. It embodies our commitment
to innovation, leveraging technology and data-driven decision-making. It develops agile
leaders and fosters a culture of excellence. It prioritizes collaboration with the joint
community while investing in robust partnerships with our allies and partners. At its core,
this plan is driven by our unwavering dedication to the health, readiness, lethality, and
success of our Soldiers and the Army.
This plan is a dynamic roadmap. Army Medicine will adapt through continuous
transformation as our environment and collective knowledge evolve. We expect each of
you to embrace and understand the plan’s objectives and how they impact your respective
organizations. We empower you to contribute to its implementation. Thank you for your
commitment to our shared culture, our united purpose, and our sacred mission. We are
honored to serve alongside each of you.
Combat Ready Care ... This We’ll Defend!
Mary K. Izaguirre

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
5
I. INTRODUCTION
The Army Medicine Strategic Plan provides a guiding framework for the U.S. Army’s Medical
Regiment. The transition of certain legacy Army Medical Command (MEDCOM) organizations
to other Army Commands (ACOMs) and the Defense Health Agency (DHA) renewed the
integration role of The Surgeon General. The Surgeon General (TSG) executes vital statutory
responsibilities under Title 10, as well as integrating health service support functions across the
joint, combined, interagency, and Army force. These responsibilities include optimizing Army
Medicine to support the mission, the Soldier, and their Families. TSG accomplishes this by
executing medical aspects of manning, training, and equipping the Total Army Medicine Force,
advising the Secretary and Chief of staff of the Army on health service support and force health
protection, and as integrator, synchronizes Army medical capabilities.
Army Medicine is grounded in providing combat-ready care optimized in support of the
mission, the Soldier, and the Family. Firmly aligned with the Army Chief of Staff’s areas of
focus, this prioritizes warfighting as the primary purpose of the Army and its raison d’être.
Since the formation of our Nation, the Army’s enduring motto, “This We’ll Defend,” has
reflected its unwavering commitment to defend the Nation. To fulfill this purpose, the Army
concentrates on four focus areas:
Warfighting: Developing the capabilities to dominate on the battlefield
Delivering Ready Combat Formations: Ensuring that units are prepared
and equipped for deployment
Continuous Transformation: Embracing innovation and adaptation to stay ahead
of emerging threats
Strengthening the Profession: Fostering a culture of excellence, teamwork, and leadership
among all personnel
By aligning with these key areas, Army Medicine will be optimized for support to the Chief of
Staff’s priorities through integrating with our Army, the Joint Force, and our Allies and Partners.
This will ensure that every Army medical professional and medical formation is trained, ready,
and integrated into a cohesive medical force.
II. STRATEGIC ENVIRONMENT
The National Defense Strategy prioritizes four key lines of effort: defending the U.S.
homeland and its hemisphere, deterring China through strength rather than force,
increasing burden sharing between the U.S. and its allies and partners, and supercharging
America’s defense industrial base. To achieve this, the Department of War (DoW) will focus
on southern border security and countering regional narco-terrorism. Simultaneously,
the DoW will deliver a ready, globally deployable force to deter China and will deepen
partnerships with “model allies” who demonstrate a commitment to collective defense and
invest in their own military capabilities. Underpinning these efforts, the Department will
lead an aggressive modernization of systems, secure supply chains, and accelerate fielding
advanced technologies to ensure a lethal, effective force.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
6
To support this, Army Medicine is investing in a transformation mindset and an agile culture
to meet emerging and future threats. Fighting near-peer adversaries, the intensity and
duration of Large Scale Combat Operations (LSCO), lack of air superiority, extended lines
of communication, contested and congested logistics, combined with the use of advanced
weaponry, create an environment with increased risk of illness, injury or death. The
physical and mental demands of sustained combat operations will take a toll on Soldiers,
increasing risk of fatigue, decreased situational awareness, and accidents or mistakes. As
a result, LSCO is projected to result in a higher number of casualties, including killed in
action (KIA), wounded in action (WIA), disease and non-battle injuries (DNBI). To mitigate
these risks Army Medicine will prioritize force health protection (FHP), develop effective
tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) for LSCO, leverage the Joint Trauma System,
improve casualty care at the point of need, enhance mass casualty operations, prepare for
prolonged care, and prioritize rehabilitation of casualties in theater.
The character of medicine is also changing, and Army Medicine will transform to provide
care to Soldiers, Families, and Retirees, both domestically and abroad, across the
continuum of competition to conflict. This transformation will address gaps in our ability
to execute evacuation, prolonged care, contested logistics, FHP, health service support
(HSS), and command and control functions in LSCO. Army Medicine will strengthen the
Army Medical Department (AMEDD) by addressing critical factors such as retention,
professional development, and recruiting challenges.
The Army Medicine landscape has shifted from the legacy structure to a more integrated
and collaborative model. As an integrator, Army Medicine has developed strong
relationships with key stakeholders, including Transformation and Training Command,
Army Materiel Command, the Army Service Component Commands, sister services, DHA,
the Joint Staff, and partners and allies to leverage innovation, inform doctrine, and ensure
integrated logistics and operational planning.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan

III. ASSUMPTIONS
Constrained Resources: The military continues to face resource pressure and must find
ways to operate effectively and efficiently to achieve objectives. We must address the
challenges of recruiting and retaining medical personnel. Both face increased pressure due
to competition from civilian healthcare organizations, job satisfaction and service identity.
The military relies on a combination of recruitment, retention, and training strategies to man
medical billets while utilizing incentives, bonuses, and educational opportunities to attract
and retain top talent.
Increasing Complexity and Uncertainty: The global security environment continues to
be complex and uncertain, with a wide range of threats emerging across multiple domains.
Alliances and partnerships will become increasingly important for the U.S., and building and
maintaining these relationships will be critical to achieving national security objectives.
Continued Advancements in Technology: Technological advancements will drive changes
in the character of warfare. The U.S. must stay ahead of the curve in developing and fielding
new technologies while leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning to facilitate
care and decisions at the speed of war. The future of warfare will be characterized by high
casualty rates in LSCO, and the U.S. must be prepared to operate effectively across all
domains (land, maritime, air, space, and cyberspace) and dimensions (human, physical, and
information) to maintain freedom of maneuver in light of increased casualties.
Transformation: Army Medicine will fully integrate with established Army processes and
ensure TSG, as the principal medical advisor to the Secretary of the Army and the Chief of
Staff of the Army, has visibility of and input to the health and medical aspects of manning,
training, and equipping the Army. Specifically, TSG provides technical advice and assistance
to the Secretariat and Army Staff (ARSTAF) for matters regarding public health, readiness
of the force, Soldier recovery care, medical force structure and equipping. TSG is also the
primary advisor for medical force development, materiel, research and development, training
and education, evacuation, and military construction.
Lt. Gen. Mary K. Izaguirre, U.S. Army Surgeon General, tours a combat casualty tent staffed by U.S. Army combat medics
and medical officers with the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team during the medical experimentation portion of Project
Convergence Capstone 4 (PC-C4), Fort Irwin, California. Team members with the U.S. Army Medical Materiel Development
Activity are assessing the progress of two programs during PC-C4: the Health Readiness and Performance System (HRAPS)
and Medical Casualty Predictive Logistics Utilization System (MCPLUS). (U.S. Army National Guard photo by T. T. Parish)

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
8
IV. CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES
Challenges:
Recruiting and Retaining Medical Personnel: Army Medicine faces challenges in
recruiting and retaining medical personnel, namely physicians, nurses, and other healthcare
professionals, due to competition from the civilian healthcare market, a national shortage
of healthcare professionals, and the changing character of the military medical enterprise.
Mass Casualty Management: The current operational environment poses significant risks
in managing mass casualties, including the need for rapid triage, evacuation, and treatment
of large numbers of wounded, ill, and injured personnel.
Medical Evacuation: Agile, multimodal medical evacuation will be required to clear
the battlefield and maximize treatment capability in LSCO. Rapid evacuation may be
complicated by near-peer adversaries, the inability to establish air superiority, distances,
terrain, and security concerns.
Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) Threats: The unpredictable
catastrophic consequences of CBRN threats pose a threat to the force and can create
mass casualties, widespread contamination, panic, and disruption of medical infrastructure
and safe patient movement.
Health Surveillance and Disease Prevention: Army Medicine maintains situational
awareness of operationally significant health threats in garrison and training environments
to ensure the medical readiness of Army combat forces. In the deployed environment,
Army Medicine must monitor and mitigate risks of endemic, emerging, and re-emerging
diseases and other health threats.
Clear the Battlefield, Return Soldiers to Duty, and Overcome Contested Logistics:
Army Medicine must provide rapid and effective treatment, evacuation, medical logistics, and

Multinational Readiness Center 25-02, at Donnelly Training Area, near Fort Greely, Alaska. The Large Scale Combat
Operations scenario used in JPMRC 25-02 helps 11th Airborne Division Soldiers and leaders develop and refine
the tactics, techniques, and procedures necessary to successfully operate in remote and extreme Arctic winter

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
9
care in austere and urban environments. Army Medicine will leverage innovative solutions,
such as telemedicine, expeditionary equipment, casualty evacuation, and enhanced
logistics, to deliver rapid and effective care. Army Medicine will also rebuild its intra-theater
rehabilitation capabilities so that Soldiers can return to the fight as quickly as possible.
Trauma Care: The nature of wounds sustained in peer conflict differs from those
experienced in counterinsurgency operations (COIN). In COIN, wound patterns are
characterized by explosive blasts, gunshot, and shrapnel wounds. In contrast, the Ukraine
conflict showed a rise in high-velocity wounds from artillery, rocket, and missile strikes.
These resulted in complex polytrauma cases with severe blast, thermal, and blunt force
wounds, coupled with psychological trauma from constant drone and artillery attacks.
Successful treatment of these complex wounds requires a well-defined, capability-based
trauma system.
Disease and Non-Battle Injuries (DNBI): DNBI historically accounts for a significantly
higher erosion of combat power and increased demand on all roles of care and medical
evacuation systems. To mitigate this impact, Army Medicine must enhance theater medical
capabilities including operational public health and equipment sets at Role 2 facilities and
rehab hospitals.
Multidrug Resistant Bacterial Infections: Army Medicine must develop effective
strategies to combat the escalating threat of multidrug resistant bacterial infections. This
particularly impacts prolonged care, delayed evacuation, rehabilitation in theater, and
potential transmission to the homeland through evacuation to military, Veterans Affairs (VA),
and civilian hospitals.
Opportunities:
Partnerships and Collaborations: Army Medicine will expand partnerships and
collaboration with academic, civilian healthcare facilities, allies, partners, and other
government agencies to leverage new technologies, share best practices, develop cost-
effective acquisition strategies, and advance the field of military medicine.
Telemedicine: Telemedicine will play a key role in Army Medicine and Joint Force
capabilities in both competition and crisis, enabling virtual consultations, monitoring, and
treatment of Soldiers in remote and austere environments.
Medical Decision Advantage Data Strategy: Real-time knowledge of battle injuries
and DNBI provides tactical, operational, and strategic advantage over adversaries. Army
Medicine’s ability to rapidly recognize and take action to mitigate conditions eroding
combat power could prove decisive in maximizing the human as a weapon system.
Machine Learning including Artificial Intelligence (AI): Leveraging machine learning
aligns with the Army’s transformation initiatives enabling Army Medicine to provide
more effective, and more efficient care to its patients, both on and off the battlefield.
Build Resilience: The Ukraine conflict has underscored the importance of grit and
resiliency in modern warfare. To instill resiliency in our Soldiers, the Army must employ
programs that build mental toughness and resilience, enhancing Soldier readiness and
performance in high-stress environments.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
10
V. OPERATIONAL APPROACH
The Army Medicine Strategic Plan focuses on five Lines of Effort, with component objectives
depicted in Figure 1. As our legacy organizations transferred to ACOMs, our focus has shifted to
integration, convergence, advising, and enabling. This strategic plan optimizes Army Medicine’s
limited resources to enable the Army’s success in current and future operational environments.
LOE 1. Recruit, Build, and Strengthen the Army Medicine Profession (Shaping). Army
Medicine implements a 21st century talent management strategy, leveraging data-driven
decision making to develop leaders and improve personnel outcomes. This approach
integrates stakeholders to foster confident and competent leaders through continuous and
deliberate training, education, and assessment. Additionally, Army Medicine will improve its
recruiting and retention efforts by optimizing job satisfaction and financial compensation for
healthcare professionals, maximizing return on investment, and enhancing quality of life for
service members and their Families.
Objective 1.1. Man the Medical Force (Acquire). Army Medicine will mitigate ongoing
recruitment and retention challenges to ensure a ready medical force. TSG is integrated with
Army human resource enterprise to optimize recruiting, training, retention, and quality of life.
Army Medicine will synchronize its efforts with Army initiatives to leverage human capital
strategy, data analytics, and legislative reform to attract and retain top medical talent.
Task 1.1.1. Develop and execute a national AMEDD Marketing Campaign to enhance recruiting
platforms (i.e. website(s), conventions attendance, and university/college visits).

LOE 2. Transform Army Medicine for MDO and the Future Fight (Shaping). Army Medicine
remains effective in and responsive to future conflicts. To achieve this, TSG ensures the Army
has the necessary medical capacity and capabilities in competition and crisis to provide
premier health service support in competition and conflict. As DoW undergoes healthcare
reform, Army Medicine will transform its formations and capabilities to meet the Army’s multi-

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
12
domain force requirements, ensuring readiness and capability for future fights. Additionally,
Army Medicine engages the appropriate Research, Development and Acquisition (RDA)
enterprise to advocate for Army requirements and funding for Science and Technology (S&T)
and Research, Development, Test and Evaluation (RDT&E) appropriations. As the operating
environment evolves, Army Medicine will develop threat-informed capabilities that enable
the 10 interrelated Army medical functions. From capability- development to planning
and programming medical field systems for the warfighter, medical force modernization
stakeholders will deliver battlefield medical capability and capacity. These capabilities will be
synchronized across the doctrine, organization, training, materiel, leadership and education,
personnel, facilities, and policy (DOTMLPF-P) continuum.
Objective 2.1. Transformation in Contact. Transformation in Contact (TiC), conducted over
eighteen to twenty-four months, focuses on prototyping organizational changes and integrating
emerging technology. This iterative process – allowing for rapid learning, failure, refinement,
and solution development – is critical for maintaining a competitive advantage. Building upon
the momentum of TiC, Continuous Transformation accelerates the implementation of objectives
outlined in the Army Campaign Plan and informs delivery of the total force envisioned in the
forthcoming Army Warfighting Concept.
Task 2.1.1. Identify and nominate medical capabilities for TiC consideration.
Task 2.1.2. Assess prototype formation design impact to medical capability and capacity.
Task 2.1.3.  Identify and message transformation activities focused on the AHS imperatives:
Clear the Battlefield, Maximize Return to Duty, and Overcome Contested Logistics.
Objective 2.2. Deliberate Transformation. Deliberate transformation uses existing Army
processes (Total Army Analysis (TAA) and PPBE) to program and build formations over the next
two to seven years.
Task 2.2.1. Incorporate medical capabilities into Army governance processes and develop
medical force modernization strategic communication.
Task 2.2.2. Synchronize DOTMLPF-P integration of capabilities across the 10 medical
functions and advocate for risk-informed resourcing in the Strategic Portfolio
Analysis Review/Program Objective Memorandum.
Task 2.2.3. Identify and submit Force Design Updates (FDUs) necessary to support continuous
transformation.
Task 2.2.4. Assess impact of the Army Structure (ARSTRUC) changes annually to the medical
force structure.
Objective 2.3. Concept Driven Transformation. Concept driven transformation looks into the
future to identify new concepts, formations, talent, doctrine, technology, or other DOTMLPF-P
changes required to compete in the future.
Task 2.3.1. Identify necessary capability or threat based assessments derived from the Army
Warfighting Concept.
Task 2.3.2. Identify and incorporate medical concept required capabilities consistent with
Army Warfighting Concept and link S&T efforts and investments to close gaps.
Task 2.3.3. Identify and synchronize experimentation outcomes with approved gaps for shared
understanding within transformation.
Task 2.3.4. Generate Army and adopt Joint Capability Requirement Documents based on
DOTMLPF-P recommendations.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
13
LOE 3. Sustain Health and Medically Preserve and Reconstitute Combat Power (Shaping).
The Surgeon General ensures the Army’s medical force can provide combat-ready Soldiers. To
address future challenges, including increased casualties and emerging threats, Army Medicine
must enhance training and advance medical research to sustain the health of our force.
Collaboration between key stakeholders supports optimization of Soldier performance and
population health through the emerging technologies and expertise. Army Medicine keeps faith
with Families, providing world-class health service support, with joint and interagency partners,
at home and abroad.
Objective 3.1. Integrate Across the Joint Medical Enterprise. Army Medicine is an essential
partner in the joint medical enterpise, integrated to develop and maintain Soldier Medical
Readiness, ensure the readiness of our deployable medical forces, and fulfill its responsibilities
to man, train, and equip the future medical force.
Task 3.1.1. Collaborate With Assistant Secretary of War for Health Affairs (ASW(HA)) and
Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower and Reserve Affairs (ASA(MR&A))
to ensure DoW health policies and programs address the Army’s Operational
Medicine (OPMED) requirements.
Task 3.1.2. Define Army provider readiness, medical R&D, disease surveillance, and blood
support requirements and assess DHAs ability to provide opportunities or
deliver support.
Task 3.1.3. Lead and advise CCMD/ASCC/ACOM surgeons to identify and meet OPMED
requirements.
Objective 3.2. Improve Installation Health Service Support. Installation Health Service
Support Plans (IHSSP) synchronize and optimize HSS and FHP in support of the installations,
formations, and Army Senior Leaders. The IHSSP’s establish measures of effectiveness and
measures of performance to inform resource prioritization, allocation, and distribution in
support of the Army Mission.
Task 3.2.1. Establish IHSSP Common Operating Picture (COP) for MTF Commanders/
Directors and capability managers.
Task 3.2.2. Assess the performance of Army IHSSP’s.
Task 3.2.3. Assess Veterinary Services mission execution (Food Protection, Animal Health
Care, Veterinary Preventive Medicine).
Objective 3.3. Optimize Soldier Performance (Lethality). The Army is focused on optimizing
Soldier performance through the application of knowledge, skills, and emerging technologies
to improve resilience, well-being, and health. This encompasses the five domains: physical
readiness, nutritional readiness, mental readiness, spiritual readiness, and sleep readiness.
TSG incorporates physical performance, nutrition, mental health, cognitive performance,
environmental health, and sleep, to optimize the Total Force Fitness through the Army’s Holistic
Health and Fitness (H2F) program.
Task 3.3.1. Build operationally relevant and standardized performance metrics and
practices to enable individual, collective, and community readiness.
Task 3.3.2. Support Soldiers to self-monitor personal performance capabilities and
capacities.
Task 3.3.3. Develop strategies to prevent and reduce Soldier performance decrements
from oath to Expiration Term of Service (ETS).
Task 3.3.4. Maximize Soldier medical readiness through collaboration with key stakeholders.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
14
Objective 3.4. Promote Population Health. Enhancing population health is a strategic
advantage that boosts the overall readiness of Army forces by preventing illnesses and injuries,
thereby maximizing operational effectiveness. Operational public health support and force
health protection activities align with Army and DoD bio-surveillance programs. Key initiatives
include anticipating and mitigating health threats, monitoring occupational and environmental
health through surveillance and epidemiology, and coordinating emergency responses through
public health emergency management and bio-surveillance. These efforts are crucial to
ensuring the well-being of the Total Army force and align with the Army Surgeon General’s
priority of Sustaining Health, which is nested within the Army’s strategic area of Delivering
Ready Combat Formations.
Task 3.4.1. Support operational public health.
Task 3.4.2. Provide public health emergency management.
Task 3.4.3. Align Force Health Protection activities with Army & DoD bio-surveillance programs.
LOE 4. Deliver Combat Ready Medical Force (Decisive). Army Medicine’s primary
responsibility is to support warfighter readiness through agile, adaptive, and responsive medical
capabilities. To achieve this, Army Medicine will assess and mitigate medical risks, integrate
medical capabilities into exercises, and coordinate with partners to ensure a combat ready
medical force. TSG plays a key role in integrating medical capabilities to provide medically
credible forces and sustain the health of the total force.
Objective 4.1. Generate Current Readiness. Army Medicine facilitates the medical readiness of
units and identifies any gaps that need to be addressed before exercises or deployments through
operational assessments. Ensures that medical units have the requisite personnel, training,
equipment, and supplies, to support generation of medical ready forces for combat.
Task 4.1.1. Develop and provide medical readiness policies, systems, and reporting mechanisms
to identify readiness lag measures and positively influence lead measures.
Task 4.1.2. AMEDD generates sufficient current readiness to meet demands for assigned,
allocated, and immediate response forces.
Task 4.1.3. Review readiness reporting to assess risks associated with personnel, training,
equipment status, and supply levels.

Objective 4.2. Generate Strategic Readiness. Strategic readiness is the Army’s ability, through
time and space, to provide combatant commanders with trained and ready units that can meet
the joint force’s operational demands. The Army measures strategic readiness by assessing seven
strategic readiness tenets (manning, training, equipping, sustaining, installations, capacities and
capabilities), as well as the Joint Capability Area (JCA) assessment for HSS.
Task 4.2.1. Integrate into the DoW and HQDA risk reporting mechanisms (e.g., Army Strategic
Readiness Assessment Inputs, Annual Joint Assessment, Joint Medical Estimate).
Task 4.2.2. Assess CLVIII HQDA Centrally Managed Programs (Medical Materiel Readiness
Program (MMRP), Unit Deployment Package (UDP), Medical Chemical Defense
Materiel (MCDM) Quarterly).
Task 4.2.3. Assess medical field system equipment fill rates across the total force quarterly.
Task 4.2.4. Assess SRC 08 readiness to meet Operation Plan (OPLAN) and Time Phased
Force Deployment Data (TPFDD) requirements.
Task 4.2.5. Assess Army Prepositioned Stock (APS) readiness for SRC 08 sets.

Army Medicine Strategic Plan
15
Objective 4.3. Theater Level, Joint Force, and Multi-National Exercises. Army Medicine plays
a crucial role in ensuring that medical capabilities are effectively employed in theater-level, joint
forces, and multinational exercises. This involves a multi-faceted approach to integrate medical
support into these complex operations, enhancing interoperability, and ensuring the health and
readiness of all participating forces. Army Medicine works closely with joint force commanders and
multinational partners to integrate medical planning into overall operational plans.
Task 4.3.1. Assess, identify, and integrate opportunities within the Joint-Exercise Priority List
(JEPL) and Army-Exercise Priority List (AEPL).
Task 4.3.2. Consolidate and distribute potential training and exercise opportunities across
Army Medicine.
Task 4.3.3. Conduct knowledge management of exercise plans, and lessons learned.
LOE 5. Strengthen Alliances and Partnerships (Shaping). Army Medicine leverages
agreements as well as collaboration and coordinating mechanisms with military and civilian
partners to meet strategic objectives. By strengthening relationships, Army Medicine
builds trust, collaboration, and interoperability that enhances the ability to provide care on
the battlefield, respond to emerging health threats, and develop novel medical response
capabilities. The interagency and inter-governmental relationships are vital to the DoD’s
success in assuring casualty care from point of injury through rehabilitation.
Objective 5.1. Execute Military-Civilian Partnerships Programs. Army Medicine creates

medical treatment facilities to sustain clinical proficiency in surgery, trauma, and critical care.
Programs with civilian partners build both individual and collective competencies, enhancing
integrated approaches and sharing of best practices. A network of MCPs that are engaged in
joint training activities enhance mil-civ interoperability which strengthens the National Disaster
Medical System.

Implementation and Assessment: The Army Medicine Strategic Plan is a multi-faceted
approach nested in the Army’s Continuous Transformation Campaign Plan, focusing on
five Lines of Effort: Recruit, Build, and Strengthen the Army Medicine Profession, Transform
Army Medicine for MDO and the Future Fight, Sustain Health and Medically Preserve and
Reconstitute Combat Power, Deliver Combat Ready Medical Forces, and Strengthen Alliances
and Partnerships. To accomplish our multiple objectives, we will track both the achievement
of outcomes and task execution. We will measure the success of LOEs and their objectives
through Measures of Effectiveness (MOEs) and Measures of Performance (MOPs), including
leadership development metrics, medical readiness rates, and alliance and partnership
engagements. MOPs track our efforts, while MOEs assess if our efforts achieve desired impact.
An assessment battle rhythm of accountability enables the Surgeon General to identify where
integration, influence, and innovation are most needed. By regularly tracking and evaluating,
we will assess plan effectiveness, identify areas of excellence or improvement, and make data-
driven policy, process, and resource allocation decisions to inform future strategy.
VI. CONCLUSION
The Army Medicine Strategic Plan provides a comprehensive framework for Army Medicine
to support the Army’s warfighting mission and ensure the health and readiness of its Soldiers.
Through the implementation of this plan, Army Medicine will prioritize force protection, develop
and implement effective tactics and procedures, foster a culture of excellence and innovation,
ultimately ensuring that Army Medicine is trained and ready in support of Army’s Mission, its
Soldiers, and their Families.
